quote: Müssen wir im gleichen Sinne auch den Fall als unrealisirbar betrachten müssen, dass sich etwas nicht beweisen (entscheiden durch endliche Zahl von Schlüssen[?] lässt)?
english: Must we in the same sense also regard as unrealizable the case that something cannot be proved (decided by a finite number of inferences)?
topic: Philosophical questions on whether human reason can answer every question it poses itself (decidability, squaring the circle, contradictory results), followed by a Plücker-type formula for the dimension of plane algebraic curves.

triage.modern_statement: This is not a specific theorem. It is a foundational question: can there be a well-posed mathematical statement that cannot be decided, i.e. neither proved nor refuted, by a finite chain of logical inferences? In other words, must every mathematical problem be solvable? In modern terms it splits into two questions. (a) Completeness: is every sentence of a sufficiently strong, consistent, effectively axiomatized theory (e.g. arithmetic) provable or refutable? (b) Decidability: is there an algorithm that decides the provability or validity of any first-order sentence (the Entscheidungsproblem)? Hilbert's question asks whether undecidability can be ruled out, in the same way that 'contradictory results' are ruled out.
triage.answered_by: Hilbert's own public answer was the optimistic 'axiom of solvability' / 'no ignorabimus' (Paris ICM address, 1900; repeated in Königsberg, 1930). The question was answered negatively by Kurt Gödel in 1931: his incompleteness theorems show there is no complete and computable axiomatization of first-order arithmetic. Alonzo Church and Alan Turing answered it negatively again in 1936, proving that the Entscheidungsproblem (formally posed by Hilbert in 1928) cannot be solved by any algorithm. It is not one of the 23 numbered problems. It is the general principle stated in the introduction to the 1900 address, and it is closely related to the 2nd problem (consistency of arithmetic) and the later Entscheidungsproblem.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's 'axiom of solvability' was his conviction that every mathematical problem can be solved by a finite number of logical steps. It is linked to the ignorabimus controversy and to the decision problem.
In his 1900 lecture Hilbert said there is 'no ignorabimus' in mathematics. He often used the phrase to express his conviction that every mathematical problem is solvable.

In the 1900 Paris address, Hilbert described rigor as the requirement of logical deduction by a finite number of processes. Together, the axiomatic method and the axiom of solvability were supposed to show there is no ignorabimus.
In 1931 Gödel proved there is no complete and computable axiomatization of first-order arithmetic. In the 1930s Gödel, Turing and Church showed that not all mathematical problems are solvable.
Hilbert posed the Entscheidungsproblem in 1928. Church and Turing proved in 1936 that no algorithm for it can exist.

triage.why: The diary question uses the same wording ('decided by a finite number of inferences', 'unrealizable') as Hilbert's published axiom of solvability. In this note he leaves it open. Publicly, he answered it optimistically in 1900 and in 1930. Gödel (1931) and Church and Turing (1936) settled it in the negative: some statements are undecidable within a given formal system, and there is no general decision procedure. The broader fields this started, logic, computability theory and independence results, are still active, but this particular question is closed. The diary page itself cannot be dated from these sources, so its exact relation to the 1900 address is not confirmed.
